summary:
The national equality body code on single-sex spaces came into force in August 2026. It requires enforcement on the basis of biological sex and gives organisations practical examples for compliance in toilets, changing rooms and similar spaces.

On 19 June 2026 Judge Lady Ross in the Outer House of the Court of Session, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, struck down the Scottish Prison Service non-statutory guidance on custody of trans prisoners as unlawful. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching gender identity rather than sex at birth. The court held that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis, addressing Equality Act 2010 Sch.22(1), the Prison Rules, the Gender Recognition Act 2004 and Article 8.

Litigation around the Scottish prison guidance included competing claims heard by the Court of Session. Counsel argued that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk. For Women Scotland challenged the guidance to require only biological females in the women’s estate, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as flexible.

British Transport Police adopted an interim position after the Supreme Court ruling on sex. Trans women are to be strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth. The prior policy had permitted trans women staff holding a Gender Recognition Certificate to intimately search women.

Police Scotland published interim guidance on 25 June 2025 for searching transgender persons. Searches involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex in custody and stop-and-search. Where lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of the individual’s lived gender on request.

In December 2023 the United Kingdom government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and United States states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium. The stated reason was that those jurisdictions allowed transition too easily. People from those locations must apply for a new certificate under British law to change legal gender in the United Kingdom.

Legal gender recognition has been available under the Gender Recognition Act 2004, effective 4 April 2005. The Act followed Goodwin v United Kingdom (2002), where the United Kingdom was found in breach of Articles 8 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights after Corbett v Corbett (1970) had prevented change of the sex marker on birth certificates. Since 2005 a transgender person may apply to the Gender Recognition Panel after two years transitioned, without mandatory sex reassignment surgery, to obtain a new birth certificate and full legal recognition of acquired sex for all purposes. A married applicant was originally required to divorce or annul the marriage before issuance, with re-registration only through dissolution and later civil partnership. Under current law a certificate will not be issued unless the spouse consents, and the marriage must be terminated if consent is refused.

TransActual UK’s Gendered Spaces Report 2025 surveyed trans, intersex and gender-nonconforming respondents. The results corroborated fears of harassment from those opposed to their inclusion in public gendered spaces. The full report was published as a PDF.

On 18 August 2026 United Nations human rights experts warned that United Kingdom revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.

Northern Ireland operates under different equality legislation. Authorities there were still assessing the impact of the Supreme Court ruling on sex at the time of the August 2026 reporting.

Same-sex marriage was legalised in England and Wales under the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013, in force 13 March 2014, in Scotland in 2014, and in Northern Ireland on 13 January 2020 after United Kingdom Parliament intervention. Civil partnerships have been available since 2005 and give most but not all rights of marriage, with recognition problems in some other countries.
tangentialFactors:
United Kingdom media coverage of trans people has been described as increasing and becoming more vitriolic since 2016 and super-charged since 2018. A 2019 study by Paul Baker found numerous press articles from 2018 and 2019 written to be critical of trans people and to cast them as unreasonable and aggressive.

ILGA-Europe rankings record a sustained fall for the United Kingdom from 1st in Europe with an 86 percent score in 2015 to 9th in 2020 with 66 percent and 22nd in 2025 with 45 percent, the third steepest drop in Europe from 2024. The organisation’s executive expressed concern about a hostile climate on trans rights fuelled by opposition groups.
localsOnly:
National Health Service England said in March 2024 that gender identity clinics would stop prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people. The halt was renewed indefinitely in December 2024 for reconsideration in 2027. In April 2025 it was reported that the service had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since the Cass Review of April 2024, with some families turning to black-market or overseas hormones. Bell v Tavistock held in December 2020 that children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers, a finding overturned on appeal in September 2021. The Tavistock Gender Identity Development Service closed in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16- and 17-year-olds transferred to adult services.

Medical gender reassignment is formally approved and available through the National Health Service or privately. A December 2002 government policy document states that transsexualism is not a mental illness. European anti-gender discrimination law was held to apply to trans people in P v S and Cornwall County Council (1996). Discrimination protections in place since 1999 were extended to all areas under the Equality Act 2010, which covers transgender youth.
outOfScopeNotes:
No poll measuring societal acceptance of transgender people specifically was sourced. Available polling figures address sexuality only, with 86 percent agreeing homosexuality should be accepted in a 2019 poll and 77 percent supporting same-sex marriage in a 2017 poll. The transgender-specific tolerance level remains unresolved in the sources.

The precise provisions of the Equality Act revisions flagged by United Nations experts in August 2026 remain not sourced beyond the warning of discrimination and exclusion risk. Their domestic legal effect is unresolved in the inventory.

Detailed findings of the TransActual Gendered Spaces Report beyond corroborated fears of harassment in public gendered spaces remain not sourced in extractable form. Enforcement outcomes tied to that harassment are unresolved.
